地方自治体が住民基本台帳などのシステム運用委託先を切り替えようとすると、委託先から高額な作業費を請求される事例などが相次いでいるとして、公正取引委員会は実態調査に乗り出す方針を固めた。独占禁止法が禁止する取引妨害に当たる可能性があるとみて、詳しく調べる。【図解】自治体のシステム運営を巡る取引妨害のイメージ
公取委は、システムの運用を委託されている国内のＩＴ大手や自治体などを対象に、聞き取りやアンケート調査を実施し、来年１月にも結果を発表する方針だ。
全国の自治体では、政府の方針に沿って住基台帳や戸籍、児童手当など２０の基幹業務システムの仕様を統一・標準化する作業を進めている。公取委によると、この作業を請け負うＩＴ大手などが自治体に対し、不当に費用を要求しているとの声が全国から寄せられている。
具体的には、標準化作業を終えた後、自治体が運用委託先を別の事業者に切り替えようとすると、ＩＴ大手から「データ移行作業費」などの名目で１億円を超える費用を求められたとの声があるという。このほか、自治体側が作業内容の説明を求めても拒まれたという声も出ている。
調査では、こうした費用が委託先の切り替えに伴う作業に見合う適切な金額なのかといった点を確認するとみられる。
公取委によると、多くの自治体で標準化後のシステム運用経費が増加し、別の事業者への切り替えを検討する動きが広がる中で、こうした行為が続いているという。自治体担当者の間では、ＩＴ大手による「手切れ金」の要求だとして問題視する声が上がっている。
自治体の基幹業務システムの統一・標準化は、２０２１年に成立した「地方公共団体情報システム標準化法」で定められた。デジタル庁によると、２０２５年度末までに全体の約７割に当たる約２万４０００システムで完了している。政府が全国で進めてきた事業で、取引妨害が疑われる行為が広がっていた可能性があり、公取委は実態の把握を進める。

title: 関東一部 5日朝に警報級大雨恐れ
body:
関東地方は今日4日(水)の夕方から雨の降りだす所があるでしょう。夜遅くなるほど雨の範囲が広がり、本降りの雨となりそうです。5日(木)は明け方から朝に雨のピークとなり、沿岸部は昼前にかけて激しい雨の降る所があるでしょう。神奈川県東部や千葉県、茨城県では警報級の大雨となる可能性があります。5日(木)の夕方にかけて土砂災害、低い土地の浸水、道路の冠水などに注意が必要です。
今日4日(水)、本州付近は高気圧に覆われますが、高気圧の中心は次第に日本の東へ移動します。関東地方には湿った空気が流れ込むでしょう。はじめ日の差す所もありますが、雲が次第に厚くなります。東京都や千葉県など関東南部では夕方から雨の降る所があるでしょう。夜遅くなるほど雨の範囲が広がって、降り方も次第に強まってきそうです。今日はお出かけの際に雨が降っていなくても、傘を忘れずにお持ちください。日中の気温は昨日ほど上がらず、最高気温は17℃前後にとどまりそうです。薄着だとヒンヤリと感じられるでしょう。
明日5日(木)は、朝までに伊豆諸島付近で低気圧が発生し、発達しながら三陸沖へ進みます。また、台風31号が父島の西を北上し、台風周辺の暖かく湿った空気が流れ込むでしょう。これらの影響で関東地方は大気の状態が非常に不安定になりそうです。5日(木)に日付が替わる頃には関東の広い範囲に雨雲がかかります。明け方から朝の通勤時には本降りの雨となり、沿岸部では昼前にかけて雷を伴って激しい雨の降る所があるでしょう。夕方にかけて土砂災害や低い土地の浸水、道路の冠水などに注意が必要です。ポイントは、雨のピークが通勤時間に重なる可能性があるという点です。特に千葉県周辺では発達した雨雲や雷雲がかかりやすく、列車の遅延など交通機関が乱れることも考えられます。明日の朝は少し早めに起きて、時間に余裕を持ってお出かけください。なお、神奈川県東部や千葉県、茨城県では、雨雲が予想以上に発達した場合や、発達した雨雲がかかり続けた場合には、警報級の大雨となる可能性があります。最新の気象情報を確認してください。

title: 1兆円盗難 バイナンスが手口公表
body:
（ブルームバーグ）:暗号資産交換業者バイナンスは、先週明らかになった63億ドル（約1兆円）相当の暗号資産盗難事件で、攻撃者が偽の採用面接などで社員をだます「ソーシャルエンジニアリング」やマルウエア（悪意のあるプログラム）を使っていたと明らかにした。事件の手口や経緯をこれまでで最も詳しくまとめた報告書を公表した。同社は今回の攻撃を北朝鮮によるものとみており、「高度で複数段階にわたる作戦」だったと説明した。3日に公表した報告書によると、同社のエンジニアの1人が求人サイトを通じ、プロジェクト責任者を名乗る人物から接触を受けた。その後、チャットアプリ上で架空企業の最高経営責任者（CEO）を装う人物の面接を受け、採用課題として悪意あるプログラムを含む開発用ファイル一式をダウンロードするよう求められた。これをきっかけに、一連の不正操作が始まったという。バイナンスのリチャード・テン共同CEOは「一度のミスや侵入で起きた事件ではなく、数カ月かけて周到に仕組まれた攻撃だった」と述べた。事件が最初に報じられた10月29日、同社は攻撃者がソフトウエアエンジニアのノートパソコンに侵入し、そこを足がかりに取引所から暗号資産を引き出した可能性があると説明していた。その後、攻撃は「複雑」で、ほかにも侵入経路が見つかったとしたものの、詳細は明らかにしていなかった。事件発覚後、トレーダーやサイバーセキュリティーの専門家、暗号資産を発行する企業などは相次いで措置を講じた。ステーブルコイン大手のテザーやサークル・インターネット・グループなどは、約30億ドル相当の資金を凍結するなどして、攻撃者による資金移動を阻止した。分析会社は暗号資産の流れを追跡し、最終的に北朝鮮の関与を指摘した。北朝鮮は関与を否定している。一方、市場の混乱に乗じて利益を得たトレーダーもいた。バイナンスは損失を自社で負担すると説明し、利用者の不安払拭に努めた。ただ、事件後はほぼ2日間にわたって出金を停止し、11月1日早朝から段階的に再開した。当初は利用者の出金が相次ぎ、数十億ドル規模の資金が流出したが、その後は落ち着きを取り戻したもようだ。3日には、1時間当たりの入金額が出金額を上回るようになったと発表した。また、自社資金と2つの保険基金を充て、流出した暗号資産をほぼ補充したとも説明している。
暗号資産史上最大のハッキングとなったものの、相場への影響は限定的だった。ビットコインは事件直後に4％超下落し、一時7万6000ドル近くまで値を下げたが、その後は下げ幅を縮め、3日には7万7000ドル台半ばで取引されている。原題:Binance Hackers Used Fake Job Interviews in ＄6.3 Billion Heist（抜粋）もっと読むにはこちら bloomberg.com/jp（c）2026 Bloomberg L.P.
Ben Weiss, Ryan Weeks

title: 北朝鮮が日本海に向け飛翔体発射
body: 韓国軍は、北朝鮮がさきほど、日本海に向けてなんらかの飛翔体を発射したと発表しました。詳しい種類や飛行距離などはわかっていません。【画像】北朝鮮“巡航ミサイルに搭載したクラスター弾の威力を評価する試験を実施”北朝鮮は10月29日にも東部・元山一帯から日本海に向けて短距離弾道ミサイルなど十数発を発射したほか、31日には戦術弾道ミサイルに搭載したクラスター弾の試験を行っています。北朝鮮が韓国との軍事境界線付近の要塞化を進めていることなどを背景に緊張が高まっていて、韓国は北朝鮮側に南北軍事会談の開催を要請していますが、北朝鮮は応じていません。

title: 米中間選挙 予測市場が試練に直面
body: Douglas Gillison　Michelle Price[ワシントン ３日 ロイター] - ３日に投開票の米中間選挙で、予測市場は民主党が米連邦議会の上下両院を制覇するとの見方を強めた。中間選挙には１４億８０００万ドルを超える資金が賭けられ、予測市場の‌信頼性が試されている。開票が始まると、賭けの価格は民主党優位の方向にさらに動いた。米東⁠部時間３日午後７時（日本時間４日午前９時）時点で、分析会社ベットイントが集計した予測市場の価格は、民主党が下院で多数派を取る確率を９８％と示唆し、同日昼過ぎから４ポイント上昇した。市場が示唆する民主党の上院制覇の​確率は大きく変動し、一時、同日序盤より１４ポイント高い８８％に上昇した。その後は８０％前後に低下した。米東部時間午後６時に最初の投票所が締め切られると、ベットイントのデータによれば、民‌主党が上下両院を制するとの賭けや、激戦となっているオハイオ、テキサス、メーンの各州の上院選、一部の知事選で民主党が勝利するとの賭けに約２００万ドルが流れ込んだ。予測市場は２０２４年、トランプ大統領が大統領選で‌勝利すると予測し、従来の世論調査に反する結果‌を示して一躍脚光を浴び、それ以来、世界中のメディアや投資家から注目を​集めてきた。これらの市場は賭けのオッズを提供する上で高い的中率をうたうが、米国の予備選やブラジル大統領選で予測を外し‌て注目された例もあったことから、誤りがあり得ることも示されている。３日に示唆された民主党の上下両院制覇も、今後詳しく検証されることになる。アナリスト‌らは、中間選挙の結果が予測市場のオッズか​ら大きく乖離（かいり）した場合、特に賭け金が過去最高額に達していることを踏ま‌えると、業界の評判が損なわれる可能性があると指摘する。最大手の予測市場プラットフォームであるカルシとポリマーケットは、複数の⁠候補者が自らの選挙戦に賭けたほか、ワシントンの非営利団体「反汚職データコレクティブ（ＡＣＤＣ）」の調査で政治市場が比較的少額の賭けで動かされ得ると判明したことを受け、不正行為の防止を迫られている。ＡＣＤＣによると、カルシは２日、全ての中間選挙関連の賭けで取引高⁠が１３億３０００万ドルに上ったと報告した。一方、ポリマーケットの議会選市場への賭け金​は約１億４５００万ドルだった。これまでに２万８０００を超える中間‌選挙関連市場が開設され、テキサス、ミシガン、メイン、サウスカロライナの各州の上院選を含む一部の個別選挙が取引高の大きな割合を占めている。例えばテキサス州の上院選には、ＡＣＤＣによると１０月２９日時点で約６７００万ドルの賭けが集まっていた。ベットイント⁠によると、３日夜時点で市場は、民主党候補のジェームズ・タラリコ氏が同州の共和党のケン・パクストン⁠司法長官を破り、この議席を獲得する確率を７５％と示唆し、同日序盤から３ポイント上昇した。２６００万ドル超の賭けが集まったミシガン州の上院選で⁠は、ベットイントによると、民主党のアブドゥル・エルサイード氏が共和党のマイク・ロジャーズ氏に勝利する確率を市場は８３％と示唆し、同日‌序盤から７ポイン⁠ト上昇した。バンダービルト大学ロースクールのイシャ・ヤダブ副学部長は「３日は確かに、新たな予測市場にとっ​て真の試金石となるだろう」とし、２０２６年は議会選が数多く行われるため、予測市場業界全体の予測精度を評価する材料になる可能性があるとの見方を示した。

title: 米中間選挙 集計長期化の可能性も
body: 【ワシントン＝本間英士】3日の米中間選挙は与党・共和党と野党・民主党による接戦が見込まれており、その場合上下両院の大勢判明には数日かかる可能性がある。郵便投票が普及している米国では、投開票日までの消印があれば投開票日後に届いても有効とみなす州もあり、集計の長期化が想定されるためだ。与党が僅差で敗れた場合、トランプ政権が選挙結果に異議を唱える事態も想定される。【画像】MAGA支持者は「超バカ」…AIが生成した金髪女性のビキニ写真で荒稼ぎフロリダ大の集計によると、2日時点で郵便投票を利用して投票を済ませた有権者数は2560万人超。郵便投票の場合は、封筒の開封や投票者の署名確認などといった作業が発生し、集計に時間を要する傾向にある。前回の2022年中間選挙では、接戦となった選挙区などの開票作業が長引き、上院の多数派が判明したのは投開票日から4日後、下院は8日後だった。今回も広大な北部アラスカ州や西部カリフォルニア州などで時間がかかると予想される。特にアラスカ州の上院選を巡っては、共和党の現職ダン・サリバン氏と、同姓同名の新人が立候補し、混乱が生じている。トランプ政権は、現職サリバン氏が僅差で民主党候補のペルトラ前下院議員に敗北した場合、現職の支持者に投票先を誤認させた可能性のある選挙結果の認定を差し止めるよう求める訴訟を起こした。同州の連邦地裁は今月1日にこの訴えを退けたが、政権側が上訴した。トランプ氏は2日、自ら改修を主導した首都ワシントン中心部の人工池の前で演説。アラスカ州の上院選について、「民主党が偽物を立候補させた。有権者を混乱させるためだ。本当に不正な選挙だ」と主張した。トランプ氏が中間選挙の結果を無条件で受け入れるかを明言していないことへの懸念もある。トランプ氏は10月27日、「公正な選挙であれば結果を尊重する」と記者団に述べ、選挙の結果次第では異議を唱える可能性を示唆した。

title: 米 イスラエル年40億ドル支援終了
body: Humeyra Pamuk　Susan Heavey[ワシントン　３日　ロイター] - トランプ米大統領は３日、イスラエルのネタニヤフ首相との合意に基づき、同国への年間４０億ドルの支援を今年末で打ち切ると発表した。ただ、中東の緊密な同盟国であるイスラエル‌への武器売却は継続するとした。この日は連邦議会の主導権を左右する中間選挙の投票日。トランプ氏⁠はイスラエル支援の打ち切りについて、イスラエルへの軍事支援を支持する共和党を左派系民主党が攻撃する際の「好都合な批判材料」を取り除く狙いもあると説明した。ただ、米国がイスラエルに年間３８億ドルの軍事支援を​供与することを定めた覚書（ＭＯＵ）の期限は２０２８年９月で、どのような手続きを経て支援を年末で終了させるのかなど、詳細は示さなかった。イスラエル支援は数十年にわたり超党派の強固な合意に支えられてきたが、‌今ではその合意は揺らぎ、イスラエル支援が一部の有権者との関係で自身の政治的な重荷になっているとトランプ氏は認めたようだ。一部のアナリストは、トランプ氏の今回の発表について選挙当日のアピールを狙った政治的な戦術‌との見方を示した。米国とイスラエルの間では、２８年以降の支援‌の在り方を巡る協議が進められており、ネタニヤフ氏もこれまでに米国の支援は時間​をかけて縮小していくとの見通しを示していた。しかしトランプ氏は、米イスラエル関係の大きな転換となる今回の方針について、既に決断したこ‌とを示唆したようだ。両国はイランへの共同攻撃から８カ月余りが経過した今も、同国との紛争を続けている。トランプ氏の発表について、米ホワイトハウスとイスラエル首‌相府のいずれもロイターのコメント要請に応じな​かった。トランプ氏はＦＯＸニュースの番組「フォックス・アンド・フレンズ」で、イスラエルはもはや米‌国の資金支援を必要としていないと説明。「米国はイスラエルに年間４０億ドルを供与してきたが、ネタニヤフ首相と私は数カ月前、これを終了することで合意⁠した」とし、「今年末までにイスラエルへの支払いをやめることで既に合意している。ただ、イスラエルが必要とする場合は支援する」と語った。トランプ氏は同時に、一部の民主党議員や左派政治家が米国によるイスラエル支援を「不公平さの象徴」として利用し、共和党を批判している⁠と主張。自身が対イスラエル資金支援の停止を表明した理由を説明する中で、激戦区​の中西部ミシガン州の上院選に民主‌党から出馬しているアブドゥル・エルサイード氏を名指しし、今回の発言の政治的な側面が強調される格好となった。エルサイード氏はイスラエル支援に反対しており、当選すれば米上院初のイスラム教徒議員になる。トランプ氏は「イスラエルは支援を必要とし⁠ていないのに、なぜわれわれがエルサイードのような正気ではない連中から非難を浴びなければならないのか」⁠と述べ、「好都合な批判材料になっている」と語った。世論調査によると、米国民のイスラエル支持はパレスチナ自治区ガザでの戦闘の影響で全体と⁠して低下している。ワシントンのシンクタンク、戦略国際問題研究所（ＣＳＩＳ）のジョン・オルターマン氏は「不可解なのはタイミングだ。なぜトランプ大統領は投票‌日に発表した⁠のか。しかも、米国とイスラエルによるイランへの大規模な共同攻撃が数日以内に行われる可能性があるとの臆​測が出ている中で、なぜ発表したのか」と述べた。共和党のドン・ベーコン下院議員はＣＮＮに「私が本当に懸念したのは、イスラエル側がこの件を知らなかったことだ」と語った。

title: 自治体システム移行費巡り調査へ
body:
地方自治体が住民基本台帳などのシステム運用委託先を切り替えようとすると、委託先から高額な作業費を請求される事例などが相次いでいるとして、公正取引委員会は実態調査に乗り出す方針を固めた。独占禁止法が禁止する取引妨害に当たる可能性があるとみて、詳しく調べる。【図解】自治体のシステム運営を巡る取引妨害のイメージ
公取委は、システムの運用を委託されている国内のＩＴ大手や自治体などを対象に、聞き取りやアンケート調査を実施し、来年１月にも結果を発表する方針だ。
全国の自治体では、政府の方針に沿って住基台帳や戸籍、児童手当など２０の基幹業務システムの仕様を統一・標準化する作業を進めている。公取委によると、この作業を請け負うＩＴ大手などが自治体に対し、不当に費用を要求しているとの声が全国から寄せられている。
具体的には、標準化作業を終えた後、自治体が運用委託先を別の事業者に切り替えようとすると、ＩＴ大手から「データ移行作業費」などの名目で１億円を超える費用を求められたとの声があるという。このほか、自治体側が作業内容の説明を求めても拒まれたという声も出ている。
調査では、こうした費用が委託先の切り替えに伴う作業に見合う適切な金額なのかといった点を確認するとみられる。
公取委によると、多くの自治体で標準化後のシステム運用経費が増加し、別の事業者への切り替えを検討する動きが広がる中で、こうした行為が続いているという。自治体担当者の間では、ＩＴ大手による「手切れ金」の要求だとして問題視する声が上がっている。
自治体の基幹業務システムの統一・標準化は、２０２１年に成立した「地方公共団体情報システム標準化法」で定められた。デジタル庁によると、２０２５年度末までに全体の約７割に当たる約２万４０００システムで完了している。政府が全国で進めてきた事業で、取引妨害が疑われる行為が広がっていた可能性があり、公取委は実態の把握を進める。

title: GMO熊谷社長ら 報酬を3カ月減額
body:
ＧＭＯインターネットのＦＸ（外国為替証拠金）取引用クラウドサービスが不正アクセスを受け、利用者とみられる個人情報が公開された問題で、同社は２日、親会社のＧＭＯインターネットグループの熊谷正寿会長兼社長ら４人の役員報酬を減額すると発表した。【一覧】サイバー攻撃で個人情報などの流出が判明した企業・団体
熊谷氏は月額報酬の３０％を３か月、ＧＭＯインターネットの伊藤正社長は月額報酬の２５％を３か月の減額とする。今年１２月分から減額する。

title: 豪が追加利上げ 18年ぶり高水準
body:
【シドニー共同】オーストラリア準備銀行（中央銀行）は3日の理事会で、政策金利を0.25％引き上げ、4.85％とすることを決めた。9月の前回会合に続き2会合連続の利上げ。燃料価格の高騰などを背景にインフレ圧力が根強いとして、年初から断続的に引き上げてきた。政策金利は2008年11月以来、18年ぶりの高水準となる。【写真】日銀、物価2％目標到達と判断　デフレ脱却目指し14年越し実現
中銀は声明で、中東情勢を背景とする燃料高が他の商品やサービス価格にも転嫁されている兆候があると指摘。さらに、人工知能（AI）関連需要の拡大が関連製品の価格を急速に押し上げ、インフレ圧力を強めているとの認識も示した。統計局が先月発表した9月の消費者物価指数（CPI）は前年同月比で4.3％上昇した。

title: フードデリバリー業界に淘汰の波
body: コロナ禍で一時乱立状態だった国内フードデリバリー業界に、淘汰（とうた）の波が押し寄せている。【ひと目でわかる】フードデリバリー主要4社の月間アクティブユーザー数競争激化で撤退が相次ぎ、現在は米系ウーバーイーツジャパン、韓国系の米企業傘下のロケットナウ、日系の出前館の3社にほぼ集約。中でもウーバーの存在感は圧倒的で、寡占化を懸念する声も出ている。「お客さまや加盟店、配達パートナーの存在があったからこそ、ここまで成長できた」。ウーバーイーツジャパンのユリア・ブロブキナ代表は10月中旬の発表会で語った。同社の日本進出は2016年。世界中に展開する強固な事業基盤や高い知名度を武器に浸透し、国内累計注文数は同月時点で10億件を突破した。米調査会社センサータワーによると、アプリ利用者数を示す月間アクティブユーザー数（MAU）は620万人で、日本国内シェアの過半数を占める。フードデリバリーは、外食を控える傾向が強まったコロナ禍で急拡大。一時は7社を超える企業が顧客獲得にしのぎを削ったが、クーポン配布などの営業戦略が重しとなり、短期間での撤退が相次いだ。今年3月にはフィンランド発祥のWolt（ウォルト）が、9月末にはKDDI傘下のmenu（メニュー）がサービスを終了。出前館も26年8月期連結決算で8期連続の最終赤字を計上するなど苦しい状況だ。これに対し、昨年1月に参入したロケットナウは、送料やサービス料がかからない「お店と同価格」の宅配を1万店以上で展開し急成長。今年9月にはアプリの累計ダウンロード数が800万件を超え、MAUでは業界2位に躍り出た。ただ、ロケットナウの参入でウーバーや出前館も「お店と同価格」での提供を余儀なくされるなど、現状は消耗戦の様相を呈しつつある。業界に詳しい有識者は「価格だけの競争になれば、資金力が潤沢な企業が市場を独占し、長期的には利用者や飲食店が不利益を被りかねない」と警鐘を鳴らす。

title: 安いもやし限界 5年で13社消える
body:
「家計の味方」として食卓を支える「もやし」業界の苦戦が続いている。2026年に「もやし」製造業者の倒産や休廃業・解散（以下、廃業）は少なくとも3件判明し、10月に事業を停止した「サイキ食品」（埼玉）を含めると4件となった。過去5年間（2022～26年）に倒産・廃業となったもやし製造業者は計13件に達する。ただ、小規模事業者も多く、水面下の撤退を含めれば、実際にはさらに多くの製造業者が市場から姿を消したとみられる。もやし業界では、以前から販売価格が「安すぎる」問題が指摘されてきた。2017年には工業組合もやし生産者協会が業界の窮状を訴える声明を公表したほか、原料豆卸の「大西商事」（2017年11月、破産）が価格転嫁できず経営破綻し、業界の厳しい実情が注目された。2022年には同協会が日本経済新聞に「このままでは生産者が消える」とする全面広告を掲載。ロシアのウクライナ侵攻を契機とする物価高を背景に価格改定は進んだものの、「もやしは安くて当然」という認識を大きく変えるには至らなかった。こうしたなか、2026年10月には埼玉県を中心にもやしを生産・出荷していた大手のサイキ食品が事業を停止した。
足元でもコスト上昇圧力は強い。財務省貿易統計によると、もやしの主原料である緑豆の輸入単価は2026年1～8月平均で前年同期比7.2％上昇した。原料豆に加え、包装資材や電力などのエネルギーコスト、物流費、人件費も上昇が続き、業績面でも影響を及ぼしている。「もやし製造」を主力とする企業のうち、2025年度業績が判明した全国約20社では約3割が最終赤字となった。さらに減益企業を含めると、全体の65％、3社に2社で業績が悪化した。業績悪化企業の割合は2021年度（75.0％）をピークに改善傾向が続いていたが、2025年度は4年ぶりに前年を上回った。他の野菜価格が高騰するなかでも、節約志向を背景にもやし需要そのものは底堅く推移している。しかし、コスト増を十分に価格へ転嫁できず、「売れているのに儲からない」状態に陥る製造業者は少なくない。利益を確保している企業でも、健康志向を背景に単価の高いスプラウトや、カット野菜・ミックス野菜などを併営し、もやし単体の低収益を補うケースが目立ち、もやしだけでは利益を確保しづらい構造は変わっていない。もやしは地域密着型の生産体制が多く、1社の撤退でも供給網に影響を及ぼしかねない。「安くて当然」を前提とした販売構造から脱却できなければ、生産者の減少は今後も続く可能性がある。「このままでは将来、価格が高騰する」というかつての警鐘は、価格の問題にとどまらず、安定供給そのものが維持できなくなる懸念に及びつつある。

title: Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash
summary: At least 69 people were killed and dozens injured in the collision south of the capital, Madrid.
body:
Óscar Puente had been under mounting pressure as opposition parties and some allies of the government called on him to step down
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente has resigned - six days after the high-speed train collision in which at least 69 people were killed and dozens injured.
He announced his decision in Congress, after giving evidence on last Wednesday's disaster near the town of Urda, south of the capital Madrid, in which a train smashed into the back of a stationary train.
"A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year," he said - a reference to January's crash on the same line which left 46 people dead.
Last week's crash was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Rescuers had to use heavy lifting equipment to get access to derailed carriages where a number of passengers were trapped
Puente announced his decision at the end of a lengthy congressional session on Tuesday evening in which he had outlined new rail safety measures and had been grilled by the opposition.
He also said: "I am not only stepping down from my position as minister of transport, but... I am also withdrawing my name from the lists for the early legislative elections."
Puente's position immediately came under scrutiny after the 28 October crash.
The main opposition, the conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox, were both calling for his resignation - as were some of the government's allies.
They argued that the minister should take responsibility for a high-speed rail system that many Spaniards now regard as unsafe and whose credibility even Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez admitted was "broken".
The opposition also criticised Puente for appearing to blame human error for the crash, claiming the minister was trying to deflect the blame from his own failings.
But, having said he was going to remain in his post just a few days ago, his resignation appears to have taken many by surprise.
The rail accident and Puente's decision have come at a crucial moment in the Spanish political calendar, with early general elections on 29 November.
Many observers see the accident as a massive electoral setback to the Socialist-led government that will make it impossible for Sánchez to defy the polls and win the election.
Puente's predicament presented him and the prime minister with a dilemma - refusing to resign might look insensitive in the wake of the accident and stepping down could look like acknowledging he and the government were at fault.
In the end, Puente opted for the second option, insisting his decision had been driven by "political dignity".
The prime minister praised his colleague who had "faced up to the situation, provided answers and solutions, and then stepped aside".
"Out of dignity. Of his own accord. Out of respect for the victims," Sánchez added.
Many Spaniards will now ask whether Puente's successors will manage to restore faith in the country's railway system.
Last Wednesday's accident involved a train run by state-owned operator Renfe with 397 passengers on board and a stationary train run by private operator Iryo, which was carrying 147 passengers.
A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.
Leakedaudio recordings publishedin Spanish media soon after the crash revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the disaster.
The three recordings of conversations between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that the Renfe train was given clearance to move even though the other train had stopped on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Listen: Audio recordings between train driver and controller
In one, a control centre operator is speaking to the driver of the Renfe train, which was having some technical difficulties.
After some exchanges, the control operator tells the driver: "Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation."
The driver replies: "At normal speed?" To which the controller answers: "Yes."
The Lateral Signalling Block is a back-up system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.
The driver of the stationary Iryo train says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost, and it is not moving.
The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.
The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.
The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.
Iryo said its carriages were "struck from behind" by the other train.

title: Seven flights across Europe targeted by suspected bomb threats
summary: Planes in Poland, Spain, Bulgaria and Italy have been checked for explosives following separate threats.
body:
Watch: Sniffer dog inspects Ryanair plane in Spain after suspected bomb threat
Seven passenger planes across Europe, two of which departed from the UK, have been inspected following a series of suspected bomb threats.
Two Ryanair flights, one originating from Dublin and the other from Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome following anonymous tips but no explosives were found, sources at the city's Fiumicino airport told the BBC.
The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian Air Force until landing. Authorities have also searched planes in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria.
While officially there is no link between them, authorities from various countries will be co-operating to assess whether this was a co-ordinated attack, designed to disrupt airspace.
The UK government described the incidents as "malicious hoax threats".
In a statement it said it had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today".
Aviation security expert Paul Mason said bomb threats on passenger planes "don't happen that frequently", which made the latest incidents "unusual".
"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told BBC Radio 5 Live. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
He said "there are a lot of processes" that the onboard crew and people on the ground must go through "to validate the credibility of the threat".
A flight may be asked to divert if the credibility of a threat "is of a certain level", Mason added, and in some cases the onboard crew may not even be advised on what the ground operators were dealing with.
Two of the four flights were en route to Warsaw Chopin airport
In Rome, sources at Fiumicino airport told the BBC police bomb disposal experts carried out standard security protocols to ensure the safety of all passengers and crew.
Inspections of the passengers, luggage, and the aircraft yielded negative results, and the alert has since been cleared.
One plane which landed in Murcia, southern Spain - a Ryanair flight coming from Manchester - was also found not to have any explosives on board, Spanish authorities said.
One passenger later said she was unaware of the bomb threat until after the plane landed.
"We weren't told anything during the flight," Sarah told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The plane stopped quite suddenly and then we were kept on the runway for around 30 minutes."
"Then the fire engines turned up, the bomb squad turned up and we were asked to evacuate," she continues.
Sarah said the plane had not been on the ground a minute before it was "surrounded by fire engines and police and a bomb squad". All the passengers were then escorted by police, leaving all their belongings.
"We were only later told that it was an actual threat, a bomb threat to the plane itself," she added.
Two flights heading to Warsaw were also affected, including one from London Heathrow.
The Heathrow flight was originally meant to land at the Polish capital's main airport, Chopin, but was diverted instead to the smaller Modlin airport, briefly forcing its closure.
A Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as planned.
Later on Tuesday, Bulgarian Transport Minister Georgi Peev said there were bomb threats against two planes travelling to the country's capital Sofia.
He told the state-owned Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) the flights were from the northern Italian city of Bergamo and Ireland's capital Dublin.
The flights into Sofia were not diverted and no explosives were found when the planes were checked, Peev said.
Bulgaria's border police said in a statement sent to the BBC that at around 10:35 (08:35 GMT) it had received an email about "the presence of an improvised explosive device on a flight returning from Bergamo".
"Standard procedures for such incidents were immediately activated, and an operational headquarters comprising representatives of various institutions was convened," the statement said.
The border police added that the same email also reported a "similar threat against aircraft arriving from Dublin".
Initial checks found no explosives on board the Crown Iris cruise ship
In a separate development, a bomb alert triggered the evacuation of 1,537 passengers and crew from an Israel-bound cruise ship in Greece, media reports from both countries say.
Initial checks of the Panama-flagged Crown Iris vessel currently docked at a port on the Aegean island of Syros found no explosives, they said citing the Greek Coast Guard, and the ship was due to resume its journey.
Tuesday's aircraft incidents come a day after a Wizz Air flight from London Lutonmade an emergency landingin Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet, after a bomb threat.
Wizz Air said later that security checks had been made and nothing was found.
BBC Verify has consulted aviation safety experts about what happens on board a plane when a bomb threat is issued.
Marco Chan, a former pilot for Cathay Pacific Airways and Hong Kong Airlines who is now a senior lecturer in aviation operations at Kingston University, said a bomb threat is considered "genuine until it is resolved, even though most turn out to be hoaxes".
Chan said crews will "quietly search" toilets, galleys and storage areas and will not touch a suspicious item unless it has to be taken to an area on the aircraft designated as the least risky bomb location.
The aircraft's captain will have multiple factors to assess, according to former airline pilot Terry Tozer, an aviation safety commentator.
He said these include what facilities are available at the airport they are being diverted to and how the plane can continue onwards should it turn out to be a false threat.
Chan added that once on the ground, the plane is generally "taken to an isolated stand, passengers are disembarked, and police and bomb disposal teams search it".

title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
summary: An engineer was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives, Binance says.
body:
Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.
Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".
It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.
Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".
In apost on X,external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.
These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts.
Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.
It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images.
The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.
Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.
The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.
Customers withdrewbillions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened.
"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.
The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.
It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.
The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be thelargest crypto hack to date.
What we know about the $6.3bn Binance hack
US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.
The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea.
Pyongyanghit back at the claims on Tuesday, denying it was behind the hack.
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image.
The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record$1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
But on Tuesday, thecompany wrote in its post on X,external: "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident."
As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also  increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident.
It also said that it would seek to stablish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives.

title: NTSB says crucial plane parts found three miles from Florida crash site
summary: The NTSB said because the parts were found far from the accident site, they fell off before the crash.
body:
The NTSB found "the majority" of the Learjet's left elevator - a control surface located on the tail - in three pieces, NTSB member Tom Chapman said
Crucial components of a private jet that crashed in Palm Beach, Florida - including a part that controlled the up-and-down movements of the nose of the plane - were found 1.3 (2 km) to 3.8 miles away from the crash site, an investigator said on Tuesday.
National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigators said they believed parts of the jet may have broken off before the Sunday crash, which killed all nine on board.
The NTSB found "the majority" of the Learjet's left elevator - a control surface on the tail - in three pieces, NTSB board member Tom Chapman said.
Chapman said because the parts were "quite some distance away" from the site, investigators determined they fell off before impact.
Three years before crash, young co-pilot spoke of earning pilot licence
"Knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us towards other things to investigate," he said.
Chapman said officials were still working out whether losing the left elevator  caused the plane to nosedive or whether the part fell off because "forces on the aircraft caused that to separate".
He said the part of the plane that controls upward and downward movement may not have been "effective" at the speed the plane was travelling.
The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas, when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.
In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".
They are then heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.
An emergency was declared and the pilots can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
NTSB plans to investigate the role weather played in the crash. Officials were struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on a road in Palm Beach.
Chapman said on Tuesday that the force of the impact severely damaged the wreckage.
Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and  Anita Maria Cetina, a nanny.
The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory. Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.

title: Libya's top religious authority rules against wearing Nike clothes
summary: The US company was named after the Greek goddess of victory, so the Dar al-Ifta said displaying its logo was unIslamic.
body:
Nike clothes are popular in Libya, although many are counterfeit
Libya's highest religious authority, the Dar al-Ifta, has issued a ruling banning Muslims from buying, selling or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo.
The ruling, issued by the Tripoli-based institution, states that the US sportswear giant was named after the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo was inspired by her wings.
It argued that wearing clothing displaying the logo amounted to promoting symbols associated "with polytheism," or the worship of more than one god.
Libya is home to the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, where archaeological remains include a statue of the Greek goddess of the same name.
The religious committee also accused Nike of supporting Israel and called for a boycott of companies that back the country.
It referred to a statement issued by its Council for Research and Sharia Studies on 5 November 2023, urging Muslims to boycott Western companies it considers supportive of Israel during the war in Gaza.
The ruling, known as a fatwa, is a religious opinion on a matter of Islamic law. It was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani.
The BBC has contacted Nike for comment.
The Dar al-Ifta is an influential religious institution based in Tripoli, in western Libya. The country is politically divided, with rival authorities and institutions operating in the east and west after years of conflict following the toppling of long-time leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
Although its religious rulings can carry considerable social influence, they are not necessarily government orders or legally enforceable.
Last year it ruled against wearing jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels, arguing that its four-leaf clover design was associated with Christian beliefs and the pursuit of good luck, which it said contradicted Islamic teachings.
The latest fatwa does not announce a state ban on Nike products or specify penalties for people who continue to buy or wear them.
Social media reactions were mixed, with some users welcoming the ruling, while others questioned its significance, describing it as ironic or a distraction from more pressing issues.
The ruling comes amid wider debates over the rise of religious conservatism in public life in Libya.
In 2025, authorities in eastern Libya announced restrictions on rap music, theatre and dance performances, citing concerns that some lyrics and performances violated public morals and Islamic values.
The measures were subsequently extended to western Libya.
The Dar al-Ifta has also previously issued religious rulings against music, although there is no clear evidence that it was directly involved in the restrictions on performances.
Nike does not operate an official store in Libya, however Nike-branded products are available through local sportswear retailers.
Sportswear brands such as Nike and Adidas are popular across North Africa.
In Libya, as in other countries in the region, counterfeit versions of popular sportswear brands are also sold in local markets.

title: Poundland supplier 'will lose millions' if retailer collapses
summary: One of Poundland's suppliers will lose millions if it collapses, while other suppliers have said they would go under.
body:
Adam Turner is sales director at Poundland supplier Hillcrest
One of Poundland's suppliers has said it will lose millions if the firm collapses.
While that supplier will stay afloat, it is feared that some small and medium-sized suppliers could go under.
This is in addition to potentially thousands of job losses among staff.
Politicians have been putting questions to representatives of Poundland owners Gordon Brothers this week seeking "clarity" on plans for the retailer.
Adam Turner, sales director at Highcrest Retail Brands - a family owned Bradford business - told the BBC that Poundland was one of Highcrest's biggest customers, and that the firms have had a relationship for decades.
Highcrest mainly sells confectionary to Poundland, and turns over about £50m.
It will "lose a few million" if Poundland becomes insolvent, so it will have a gap in its balance sheet next year, he said.
Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", but other medium and small suppliers have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they", Mr Turner said.
This echoes awarning from Poundland founder Steve Smithon Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse.
Not only 12,000 Poundland staff would be affected, but also potentially tens of thousands more, he said.
If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises. However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present - meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed.
Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm
Mr Turner said that the last three months of the year is the "golden quarter" for retailers. In terms of sweets, Poundland will get its Halloween stock in from July, and Christmas stock in from September.
These three months will be the time of year when suppliers will be owed the most by Poundland.
If Poundland goes under, suppliers will be getting "pennies in the pound" back from the administration, he said, which is "very upsetting" - although he still hopes a deal can be done so Poundland can remain solvent.
Poundland owners Gordon Brothers will be a secured creditor, which means they are first in line to get their money back, and suppliers "who have done nothing wrong" will take the financial hit.
"It's sad. It's a nightmare for us all to be honest with you. It's not just the suppliers, it's the staff at Poundland, some of these guys have been there for many years.
"It's from the warehouse staff all the way to the shop staff to everybody within head office. It's a massive ripple effect through the supply chain," he added.
Mr Turner said he had no knowledge of whether Gordon Brothers had deliberately timed the process of Poundland going into administration so it could take advantage of having high stock levels, which it can then sell.
One of the ways Gordon Brothers makes money is through stock liquidations - selling off stock from collapsed businesses.
One insider familiar with the situation told the BBC that the timing of Poundland facing collapse was "odd" - most retailers don't fall over in the run-up to Christmas.
Gordon Brothers was approached for comment.
Meanwhile, business secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet with Gordon Brothers later this week after he and Prime Minister Andy Burnham questioned why a solvent deal had not been made.
Business minster Kate Dearden told MPs that government officials had also met with representatives from Gordon Brothers on Monday.
"I am deeply concerned about the uncertainty surrounding Poundland's future and the impact it could have on its staff and their families who are at the forefront of my mind," Dearden told the House of Commons.
"Poundland is not currently in administration and the business continues to trade, but this is a worrying time for employees, suppliers and communities", she added.
The minister confirmed she would also be meeting with Poundland executives on Wednesday.
She said the government doesn't want to interfere with "current ongoing commercial negotiations", but said ministers would be seeking "clarity" on the plans for the retailer.
"It's absolutely legitimate for this government to ask the business if they're doing everything they can to protect employees and suppliers up and down the country," she added.
Dearden told MPs that the government would be ready to help the company's employees, should the current situation end in administration.
"We stand ready to support them if they need to move into new employment, however... our priority is always in protecting jobs and the Secretary of State and I will continue to engage with the company to secure the best possible outcome," she added.
The head of Gordon Brothers' European operations reportedly told the government that the firm stood by its stewardship and had given Poundland £85m in additional financing since its purchase in 2025.

title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
summary: The food deal, ahead of a UK-EU summit later this month, is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far.
body:
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.
The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.
Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.
The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.
As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.
Speaking during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the prime minister said a UK-EU deal could add up to 0.4% extra on GDP.
The deal could have the following impact:
Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume
It should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm  the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to
It should also end the need for £25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases
Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed
It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU
In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment".
Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.
Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.
At Chogm on Tuesday, Burnham said: "I think people in Britain would expect me to take that with both hands, given where we've been in recent times, and that's what I'm doing."
Pressed on whether it would be acceptable for the UK to have its rules on food trade made by the EU, he said: "We're not in the EU, therefore we do have to work with them in a different way.
"But if that can get growth, if that can help our farmers, if that can remove red tape from British businesses, I think most people would expect me to go to that summit and negotiate the best deal that I can.
"And that's what I've been doing in recent weeks, leaning in, being positive, having a really constructive relationship with our European partners and hopefully we can land a good deal for Britain in terms of growth but also I hope more collaboration on controlling immigration."
Jon Walsh of Bio&Me said his firm had stopped exporting yoghurt due to vets' fees
Jon Walsh, the chief executive and co-founder of Bio&Me, which makes granolas, mueslis and yoghurts, told BBC 5 Live the draft deal sounded like "really good news".
"We're just a small company but when we were trying to export our yoghurts before, every time we'd send a pallet we had to pay a vet to inspect it and that was £140, and that meant that you'd lose money... so we had to stop."
The company also had problems exporting granola and overnight oats, with some shipments being returned.
"It was so frustrating because it was the same person filling out the same form and yet half would make it through and half wouldn't," Walsh said.
"You just kind of give up because you're losing money."
In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue.
"The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added.
Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU.
Asked by the BBC about the UK's relationship with the EU, Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch said that while we should "work closely", "dynamic alignment" with the EU would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".
Liberal Democrat Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said the draft deal was a "patch, not a fix".
"The real solution is to rejoin the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU," he added.
Reform UK's business spokesman Richard Tice said: "One of the key benefits of Brexit was that Britain no longer had to adhere to ridiculous EU rules.
"Returning to any form of alignment with Europe would crush Britain's competitiveness and force us to surrender sovereignty over trade policy, putting trade deals worth hundreds of billions of pounds at risk."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen with Prime Minister Andy Burnham
While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force.
The government has already announced aEuropean Partnerships Billwhich will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax.
The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets.
The BBC understands the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence co-operation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances overthe EU's "Made in Europe" plans.
A food deal will have particular significance for Northern Ireland, radically reducing the impact of the post-Brexit Irish Sea border.
Northern Ireland's Brexit deal kept it inside the EU's single market for goods. That means food products from elsewhere in the UK require paperwork and some physical checks when arriving at NI's ports. A deal will ultimately end those requirements.
While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays.
But William Bain, the British Chamber of Commerce's (BCC) head of trade policy, told the BBC's Today programme that business overall thought it was a "price is worth paying" to follow common rules, as companies would benefit from "lower costs, reduced delays [and] increased market access".
At the moment, he said, the requirement for Export Health Certificates can add thousands of pounds of costs to each truck carrying goods, in addition "to the delays that people find at the ports or at the borders".
"So we get lower exports because of the delays and the massive increases in costs that have come into the supply chain."
The BCC has released a new analysis of its members' views suggesting options for a closer relationship.
The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.

title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
summary: An engineer was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives, Binance says.
body:
Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.
Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".
It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.
Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".
In apost on X,external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.
These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts.
Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.
It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images.
The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.
Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.
The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.
Customers withdrewbillions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened.
"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.
The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.
It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.
The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be thelargest crypto hack to date.
What we know about the $6.3bn Binance hack
US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.
The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea.
Pyongyanghit back at the claims on Tuesday, denying it was behind the hack.
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image.
The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record$1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
But on Tuesday, thecompany wrote in its post on X,external: "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident."
As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also  increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident.
It also said that it would seek to stablish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives.

title: Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'
summary: CEO Melanie Perkins says more than 1,000 staff will either lose their jobs or be asked to change roles.
body:
Canva co-founder Melanie Perkins says this year has been "our hardest" yet
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.
The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.
It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.
The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.
"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."
The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.
Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.
Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.
"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.
The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.

title: Drivers may get compensation offers before car finance saga ends
summary: The regulator says it supports lenders offering early compensation offers, as long as they are fair.
body:
Drivers may be offered compensation from lenders ahead of the next legal battle in the car finance mis-selling saga.
Regulator the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it would welcome lenders making settlement offers as long as customers were not given a worse deal than under its proposed central scheme.
That scheme is facing a legal challenge, to be heard in February, with resulting compensation unlikely to be paid until late next year.
But Barclays has confirmed it will make early compensation offers from now, with others expected to follow suit.
The FCA said it would still only expect a minority of claimants to be made early offers, with most having to wait for the outcome of next year's court case.
Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA's general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said: "Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. It's clear they want the choice.
"Anyone who wants to wait can, and there's no obligation to agree to the offer. We'll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means."
The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest.
But millions of drivers who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024 will be entitled to compensation after the loans were mis-sold.
They mostly related to when car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them.
Average compensation payouts of about £829 are expected to be made related to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period.
Car finance compensation payments delayed until next year
Compensation will cost the industry up to £9.1bn, including administrative costs. Individual payouts will vary, depending on the degree of harm each driver faced.
With huge compensation payouts inevitable, some lenders have already set aside millions of pounds to cover the cost.
Barclays has decided to start making compensation payments early, potentially to start clearing the cost off its balance sheet. It pointed out that claimants had already faced "a considerable wait".
"By making these early settlement offers, we are giving some customers the option of receiving redress sooner, rather than waiting for the legal challenges and any subsequent FCA action to conclude," said a Barclays Partner Finance spokesperson.
"Each offer will be calculated using the FCA's redress scheme methodology. We will clearly explain how it has been calculated and what accepting a full and final settlement means, so customers can decide whether accepting the offer is right for them."
The lender said claimants would start to be contacted directly "in the coming weeks".
But it stressed not all customers whose complaints were acknowledged on or before 1 October 2026 would receive an early settlement offer.
The FCA has publisheda factsheet to help drivers,externalwork out whether they should accept early settlements from lenders.
It will include a list of lenders who are making early offers, to ensure claimants with other lenders are not scammed.
The regulator said lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes:
Being able to keep any payment, even if the final settlement under the central scheme after the legal challenges proved to be smaller
Claimants would not be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge meant they would have been paid more
Accepting an offer takes you out of the scheme and stops any further input from the financial ombudsman
The Finance and Leasing Association, which represents lenders, said: "We want to see consumers receive the fairest outcome in as timely a way as possible and recognise that, in some cases, that may point to early settlement, while in others it may be appropriate to await greater legal certainty."
But Kevin Durkin, solicitor advocate and director at HD Law, who represented Marcus Johnson who won his case in the Supreme Court, said he had "real reservations" that fair compensation would be offered.
"These are only heightened by reports that just a small number of claimants will receive what could be lowball offers. I fear this is crumbs from the table, for some customers who are highly likely to be owed more, while the vast majority will receive no offer at all," he said.
The main proposed FCA scheme remains partially suspended, pending legal challenges in February.
Consumer group Consumer Voice said the proposed compensation scheme left "too many people short-changed". Three lenders - Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance - are also challenging the scheme.
The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled from 16 February to 3 March.
Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained can still complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website onhow to complain for free,external.

title: Mahmood refuses to put cost on care worker settlement climbdown
summary: The home secretary says the full cost of dropping plans to extend the wait for settlement will be laid out in future.
body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood revised her settlement reforms after a backlash from some Labour MPs
The home secretary has declined to specify how much scrapping her plan to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait longer to qualify for permanent settlement will cost.
Shabana Mahmood had originally proposed doubling the wait from five years to 10 for most migrants, with some facing a 15-year wait, which the Home Office suggested could save £10bn.
But under revised plans described by the Tories as a "U-turn", some foreign care workers will continue to wait five years, and others will be able to seek a five-year extension.
While not detailing the cost of the revised plans, Mahmood told the BBC they would still save "billions" because workers in other sectors would have to wait longer.
In March,the Home Office said,externalthe net lifetime cost of care workers and their adult dependants expected to settle between 2026 and 2030 was estimated at £10bn under existing rules.
Mahmood was proposing to delay settlement for this cohort in response to concerns over record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Tory government - dubbed the "Boriswave" by critics.
She had previously argued that not delaying settlement for migrant care workers already in the UK would lead to a "£10bn drain on our public finances".
Following a backlash, Mahmood announced on Monday that care workers who arrived in the UK before May 2025 and earned at least £25,000 a year would continue to qualify after five years, alongside some other groups.
Foreign care workers who do not qualify for the five-year settlement will be able to apply for a new five-year visa, and then seek settlement.
Just over 500,000 people will now be delayed from gaining permanent residency, down from almost 800,000 before Monday's changes. Some 1.9m people will settle in the UK between 2026 and 2030, according to the Home Office.
Indefinite leave to remain (ILR), also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship.
Asked about the cost of her revised plans, the home secretary told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the detailed costs would be published when her department puts the changes before Parliament.
In an interview recorded on Monday evening, she said the changes overall represented "savings in the billions" to the Department of Work and Pensions in people not claiming benefits.
"The reason for that is the cohort that was most likely to fall upon the state is that cohort of care workers not doing care work at the moment - if they'd settled at five years, many more of those would have gone on to claim benefits.
"That will now not happen because they will not be settling at five years - those individuals get a second chance to make that contribution that they originally came to make," she told Today.
The Home Office's £10bn figure was based on an estimate by the Migration Advisory Committee of how much an average migrant care worker would cost the UK in benefits and public services throughout their lifetime.
While Mahmood would not give a new savings figure, Home Office minister Anna Turley told BBC Breakfast it would be "at least £1bn over the next couple of years in terms of welfare savings" but "we'll be doing more calculations" on the total.
The Conservatives said the "U-turn" would cost the UK billions of pounds.
Most people who come to the UK do so legally, after being granted a visa before they travel.
A visa gives someone permission to enter or stay in the UK for a specific purpose, such as work, study or joining family members.
There were 727,487 people who came to the UK via visas from July 2025 to June 2026, not including visitors or people transiting through the UK. This was down by 15% on the same period the previous year.
That does not mean all those people travelled to the UK, only that they were approved to do so.
The most common type of visa people came to the UK on was study, which made up 53% of all visa entries from July 2025 to June 2026.
People from China were the most common group to come to the UK on study visas, making up 23% of the total.
Together, people from China and India accounted for nearly half of all study visas. This has been the case for many years.
The £10bn figure has been criticised by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), whichfound a £115bn addition,externalto UK public finances under current settlement rules.
"Public debate has focused heavily on the costs of recent migration, but this is not the whole story," IPPR associate director Marley Morris said.
Mahmood also declined to say whether Prime Minister Andy Burnham had told her to change tack on her proposals, which she had put forward in November under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.
She told Today a public consultation had resulted in a "transformative package" that "strikes the right balance".
She has denied Monday's move was a U-turn, and said the revised plans meant some 500,000 people already in the UK would now have to wait longer than five years to qualify for settlement.
The exact wait will varybased on income and whether people arrived in the UK legally or illegally.
Mahmood had faced criticism within the Labour Party for proposing to retrospectively change the rules for migrant workers already in the UK.
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner had saidit amounted to "chang[ing] the goalposts", while several MPs described the retrospective approach as "un-British" and warned it could worsen the UK's skills shortage, particularly in the care sector.

title: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
summary: Angela Rayner previously said plans were "un-British" and ministers shouldn't shift "the goalposts".
body:
Shabana Mahmood has backed down on two elements
Today's announcement has long been viewed in government as a potential political banana skin.
When the home secretary announced her first version of changes to the settlement system last year, many Labour MPs, including the housing secretary Angela Rayner, voiced their concerns about the plans.
But there was a feeling that Sir Keir Starmer's government was determined to plough on regardless. Shabana Mahmood herself repeatedly expressed how important she believed the reforms were.
But the change of prime minister over the summer gave renewed hope to those unhappy Labour MPs that they could force the Home Office into two changes.
Firstly, social care workers – under the original plans many social care workers would have had to wait 15 years before becoming eligible for settlement.
Secondly, the retrospective nature of the plans – some MPs were uncomfortable at the idea of someone coming to the UK and expecting to be eligible for settlement after five years, but then having to wait longer.
Angela Rayner described that as "un-British" and said the government shouldn't be shifting "the goalposts".
She returned to the cabinet under Andy Burnham as housing secretary and chose to repeat those criticisms in an interview during the Labour Party conference in September.
That was seen as evidence that a debate inside the top levels of government about whether to water down the plans was well and truly rumbling on.
For all the Labour MPs who wanted a change, there were others, particularly those in Brexit-supporting areas, who wanted the home secretary to stick the course.
Some inside government felt nervous about providing what they saw as catnip to Reform and the Conservatives.
All of that added up to one of the more difficult decisions that has had to be taken since Burnham walked through the doors of Number 10.
In the end ministers chose to water down the proposals for care workers – those who arrived before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year will qualify for settlement in five years.
But the retrospective nature of the plans, the thing Rayner described as shifting "the goalposts", hasn't changed.
Despite that, the majority of Labour MPs pulled their punches whenMahmood made a statement in the House of Commons earlier.
Perhaps the strongest pushback came from Rachael Maskell, who is no fan of the retrospective element - but others on the left of the party, including John McDonnell and Diane Abbott, were critical without being scathing.
Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers
What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
Outside the Commons chamber, the mood among Labour folk was pretty similar to what was said from the green benches.
One would-be critic said that while they personally still had concerns about the plans announced today, they believed the Home Secretary had successfully taken the political sting out of the situation for now.
They said the campaign by MPs and unions had led to a "big win" on settlement for social care workers, but said they were still expecting to hear from constituents negatively affected by the new rules.
One Number 10 source praised Mahmood's "take no prisoners" performance in the chamber, argued she had "found the right balance" and said the announcement had gone down as well as could be expected with Labour colleagues.
Of course, the home secretary will still need to deal with criticism from other parties.
Her opposite number for the Conservatives, Chris Philp, accused Mahmood of a significant U-turn.
Philp highlighted a claim she had previously made – that allowing care workers to reach settlement more quickly could cost the UK £10bn.
The social care workers plans announced todaywill see around 500,000 people have their path to settlement delayed, that number would have been around 800,000 under the original plans last year.
In an interview with the BBC, Mahmood wouldn't say what sort of financial burden her watering down would result in.
She also refused to confirm whether Burnham had directly asked her to water down the plans.
They are tricky questions that she will have to navigate over the coming weeks.
But the general view within government is that this is one political hurdle that has been successfully jumped.

title: Reform UK councillor charged with rape and sexual assault
summary: The Crown Prosecution Service has charged George Madgwick with 35 offences, including 12 counts of rape.
body:
George Madgwick is the leader of Reform UK in Hampshire
The leader of Reform UK in Hampshire has been charged with 35 offences against four victims over a 13-year period, including 12 counts of rape.
The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said it had charged George Madgwick with the offences, which it said took place between 2008 and 2021 in Portsmouth and Wales.
It said the 37-year-old faced charges including rape, sexual assault, controlling or coercive behaviour, and making indecent images of a child against four victims - who were aged 16 and 17 at the time.
Madgwick, who is due to appear at Portsmouth Magistrates' Court on 25 November, denies any wrongdoing. Reform UK said he had been suspended from the party "with immediate effect".
In a statement posted on social media on Tuesday evening, Madgwick said: "I am shocked and dismayed at the charges brought against me.
"Whilst the charges are extremely serious, I will say unequivocally that I am innocent of the allegations against me.
"Due process must take its course and the legal process must be followed without hindrance."
He said he will continue as an independent councillor on Hampshire County Council and Portsmouth City Council.
Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said its investigation into Madgwick began on 24 July 2025, after receiving a report of a sexual offence.
The force said it first arrested him on 6 January 2026, before he was charged by the CPS on Tuesday.
Reform UK's Hampshire leader charged with rape
In total, Madgwick, who is from the the Anchorage Park area of Portsmouth, has been charged with 12 counts of rape, two counts of assault by penetration and two of sexual assault.
Madgwick has also been charged with two counts of making indecent images of children, two of controlling or coercive behaviour and eight of assault occasioning actual bodily harm.
He faces one charge each of causing or inciting sexual exploitation of a child, distributing an indecent image of a child, stalking, making threats to kill, false imprisonment, theft and criminal damage.
A spokesperson for the CPS said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence and that it is in the public interest to bring the case to court.
"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are now active and that he has the right to a fair trial. There should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in any way prejudice these proceedings."
The councillor represents North East Havant on Hampshire County Council and Paulsgrove on Portsmouth City Council.
Madgwick was elected to his position on the county council by a large margin in May - just months after he was first arrested by police.
In a statement, the local authority said it was aware of the "extremely serious allegations" and that "as criminal proceedings are now under way, it would not be appropriate" to comment further.
It added that being charged with a criminal offence did not disqualify a councillor, such as Madgwick, from office.
Last month, he featured in the the ITV News Exposure documentary Undercover: A Year In Reform - after which he accused the broadcaster of  "electoral interference".
In the programme, he was shown voicing support for the Portsmouth Patriots anti-immigration group.
He subsequently issued a statement saying the undercover reporters potentially had an "impact on the result" of council elections.
